title: On Relativity Theory and Openness of the Future
relevance: Constructs a relativistically appropriate notion of becoming/open future and rebuts inference from absence of global present to determinism.
section_locator: Printed theorem on p. 149 (not p. 150): reflexivity, transitivity, invariance under time-orientation-preserving automorphisms, one past-pointing (timelike or null) related pair; the four conditions (i)-(iv) are on pp. 148-149; p. 150 removes the no-unit stipulation. The displayed theorem omits condition (iv), which the proof uses.
assumptions: The background proposal takes the here-now point as reference; definiteness is transitive and reflexive; condition (iv) leaves some states unsettled at each point. The printed theorem on p. 149 lists reflexivity, transitivity, time-orientation-preserving automorphism invariance and one past-pointing related pair, but omits both condition (iv) and causal-past inclusion. The prose on p. 149 adds that every event in the causal past (timelike or null) is definite as of the point. Condition (iv) alone is not enough: the reflexive strict chronological past is non-universal yet omits past-null pairs.
conclusion: Stein argues that SR can support an event-relative causal-past account of definiteness/open future, rather than requiring a global present. Read the p. 150 OCR sentence only in light of the preceding full-causal-past premise and unsettled condition (iv); do not cite the isolated four-premise implication as a valid characterization. The paper does not establish physical indeterminism or objective passage.
proof_status: Printed JSTOR page images inspected pp. 148-150 on 2026-10-21. The theorem is on p. 149; it includes reflexivity and the dimension qualification. The isolated display omits condition (iv) and causal-past inclusion; the universal relation refutes the display, and the reflexive strict chronological past refutes the display plus (iv). The prose supplies causal-past inclusion on p. 149. Four items remain distinct: displayed theorem, non-universality (iv), causal-past inclusion, chronological-past inclusion. No formal reconstruction of the broader argument.
open_questions: How exactly are local becoming relations generalized in curved spacetimes and stochastic dynamics?
limits: The literal theorem display is not a self-contained characterization; cite it with both condition (iv) and causal-past inclusion, or not at all. The reflexive chronological-past counterexample is exact. No broader error in Stein's paper is inferred. The scan is a JSTOR image kept local and not committed.

title: Causal Theories of Time and the Conventionality of Simultaneity
version: Noûs 11(3), Symposium on Space and Time (September 1977), pp. 293–300; DOI 10.2307/2214766. The accessed university-hosted PDF is a JSTOR scan of the published article.
relevance: Uniqueness result for simultaneity definable from causal connectibility plus an observer worldline; assumption-sensitive result often invoked in presentism debates.
limits: Proposition 2 concludes Simo or universal; the non-universal restriction is needed to select Simo. No independent proof audit/formalization, and no unconditional physical or ontological conclusion.
section_locator: Sections 1–3: Proposition 1 (p. 296); Proposition 2 statement and proof (pp. 297–299); Proposition 3 (p. 299); definitions of K and observer worldline O (pp. 294–296).
assumptions: Minkowski spacetime R⁴ represented by symmetric causal connectibility K and an inertial observer worldline O. Proposition 1 explicitly first-order defines standard simultaneity Simo from K and O. Proposition 2: if S is implicitly definable from K and O, an equivalence relation, and relates a point on O to a point off O, then S is either Simo or universal; adding non-universality selects Simo. Proposition 3: if S is implicitly definable from K alone, is an equivalence relation, and relates two distinct points, then S is universal.
conclusion: The paper establishes a mathematical uniqueness/definability result under the stated causal-connectibility, observer-worldline and relation conditions. The causal theory of time supplies a separate philosophical criterion connecting definability with non-conventionality; Malament expresses sympathy with skepticism about that criterion. The result does not unconditionally refute conventionalism or settle temporal ontology.
proof_status: Published primary scan read through Sections 1–3, definitions, propositions and proof sketches. The elementary arguments were inspected but not independently reproduced or formalized.
dependencies: Minkowski model (R⁴,K), symmetric causal connectibility, and an inertial observer worldline O; the philosophical non-conventionality inference additionally depends on the causal theory of time.
open_questions: How should implicit definability/invariance be physically motivated, and does it warrant the causal-theory bridge from mathematical definability to non-conventionality?

title: Time and Physical Geometry
relevance: Influential Rietdijk-Putnam route from special relativity to block-universe/eternalism and critique of objective becoming.
section_locator: Full article pp. 240–247, especially thesis (1) and Principle III, “There Are No Privileged Observers” (pp. 241–242); observer-overlap application (pp. 242–243); future-contingent truth discussion (pp. 243–246); transitive-closure argument and abundance-of-observers premise (pp. 246–247). Primary scan route recorded in reading_history.
assumptions: Putnam states the ontological thesis that all and only things existing now are real, then invokes Principle III (no privileged observers): if a physical relation R to me-now marks what is real and you-now is real, the same R criterion applies to you-now. R is required to be tenseless, coordinate-independent, and not selected by the initial realness extension. The SR application transfers reality through overlapping observer nows. The broader closure argument uses the transitive closure of observer-coordinate simultaneity plus an abundance-of-observers premise, including physical systems/fields. This ontological bridge is distinct from the geometric transitivity of Einstein simultaneity.
conclusion: Putnam argues from the observer-neutral reality-transfer bridge and observer-network closure to reject a past/present/future ontological asymmetry and adopts a block view. This conclusion is not entailed by Lorentz kinematics alone. His future-contingent truth-value discussion is a separate, stronger step and should not be conflated with eternalism or determinism.
proof_status: Second-pass audit read the primary paper across pp. 241–247, including Principle III, its application and the general closure discussion; no independent formal proof reconstruction. The earlier first-pass record only inspected pp. 240–242 and used an imprecise transitivity shorthand.
open_questions: How defensible is Principle III as an observer-neutral existence bridge, and what restrictions on the observer network/license for closure are justified? How does the future-contingent truth discussion depend on further assumptions?
limits: This is Putnam’s argument, not a consequence of SR alone. Preserve the distinction between Principle III, geometric simultaneity transitivity, the later transitive-closure/observer-abundance argument, determinism and future-contingent truth.

title: Presentism as an empirical hypothesis
relevance: Challenges assumption that all presentism is empirically idle; advocates a physically testable variant.
limits: The accessible public copy is not publisher-hosted and was not collated against a publisher version-of-record file. The proposal supplies no concrete detector protocol or quantitative signature; a dynamics-grounded present does not by itself decide whether past/future entities exist or whether passage is objective.
version: Philosophy of Science 80(5) (December 2013), pp. 1101–1111; DOI 10.1086/673897. Complete public PDF copy carries the journal pagination and copyright/imprint; metadata checked against Duke and Cambridge records.
section_locator: Full journal-paginated text: opening premises P1/P2 (pp. 1101–1103); shared spacetime-unity assumption and law-constitutive alternative (pp. 1103–1105); empirical system extent and revised presentist formulation (pp. 1108–1110); conclusion (p. 1110). Accessible PDF copy: https://a7ad7762-bf80-40ab-9c06-f74d25597b55.filesusr.com/ugd/766654_811c433ef66645b68a25658f93370442.pdf.
assumptions: Brading presents the familiar presentist premise (only what exists now is real) alongside the completeness of special relativity for spatiotemporal structure. She retains SR completeness but rejects the shared assumption that spacetime itself grounds ontological unity. Her alternative sketches dynamical laws as the ground of a system’s unity; a system’s present is the spatiotemporal region needed to sustain its dynamics and its extent is an empirical matter.
conclusion: Brading proposes a law-constitutive presentist alternative that avoids making a global simultaneity slice the ground of what exists. She says the view needs substantial elaboration and may be defeated if the whole universe is the only genuine dynamical system. This is a philosophical proposal, not an established empirical result, quantitative discriminator, or selection of an ontology.
proof_status: Complete 11-page journal-paginated public PDF copy read at the argument level; bibliographic metadata cross-checked against Duke author-institution and Cambridge journal records. The copy host is not the publisher; no publisher-file collation, independent Newton interpretation audit, or argument proof audit.
dependencies: Brading’s Newtonian law-constitutive unity discussion; special-relativistic spatiotemporal structure; no new physical dynamical model is supplied.
open_questions: What independently specified physical theory, system criterion and measurement would test the proposed subsystem sizes? How are overlapping dynamical systems’ local presents unified?
